**On Handwriting**

There's something quietly miraculous about handwriting. Every person carries within them an invisible template—slants, loops, pressures—that produces marks no one else can replicate, even when we all learned from the same ruled lines in childhood workbooks. Your handwriting is a kind of fingerprint made deliberately, chosen by your muscles and habits rather than chance.

I think about how much handwriting holds beyond the words themselves. A letter written quickly shows impatience in its tapering lines. A note written carefully, perhaps for someone loved, reveals itself in the steadiness of each stroke. We can read hesitation, exhaustion, joy—the emotional weather of the moment the pen touched paper. Typing flattens all of this out. A text message says "okay" whether it's sent in fury or delight; a handwritten one might press so hard into the page that you can feel the word from the back.

Handwriting is also fragile. It changes as we age, wobbles when our hands shake, and disappears entirely with us. Grandmother's recipes annotated in cursive, a father's marginal notes in a shared book—these become relics faster than we expect. Future historians may find our era strangely anonymous, billions of messages rendered in identical fonts.

So write something by hand today. A grocery list counts. So does a line in a card, or your name signed slowly enough to actually look at it. You're practicing one of humanity's oldest technologies of presence—the proof that a specific hand, attached to a specific mind, was here, and it meant this.
